item.content:encoded:
[(Kevin Buzzard says) This is a guest post by Mitchell Taylor, a mathematician who gave a talk at Imperial’s PDE seminar a few weeks ago on the topic below. If you had shown me this blog post in 2024 and told me that this is what life would be like in 2026 I suspect I would not have believed you. Now over to Mitchell.]

Recent advances in artificial intelligence have made it possible for mathematicians to formally verify their papers in Lean. This post will explain how I became interested in formal verification and how I use Lean as a tool to improve my research. It will also provide a link to a precise list of instructions that any mathematician (with a subscription to a frontier AI model) can use to verify their own results.

1. What is Lean and why do I use it?

Lean is a functional programming language and proof assistant designed for writing mathematically precise definitions, statements, and formal proofs. It is not the only such language, but it is the most popular among mathematicians. The main reason I use Lean is that a large body of formally verified mathematics has already been collected in Lean’s mathematical library, Mathlib. This library comprises over two million lines of carefully curated code, covering most of undergraduate mathematics, a substantial portion of graduate school, and selected research topics.

1.1. How I got interested in Lean

Throughout my mathematical career, I have tended to choose people to work with rather than problems to work on. My interest in Lean is no exception, as it arose naturally from interactions with my collaborators Jaume de Dios Pont, Lukas Liehr, and David Muñoz-Lahoz.

Jaume and I were both postdocs at ETH Zürich from 2023 until the end of 2025. It didn’t take me long to realize that Jaume was extremely smart, but it did take me a while to process his enthusiasm for AI. Looking at the abilities of ChatGPT at the time, I could not imagine AI being able to do research-level mathematics. However, Jaume had worked at Microsoft Research in the summer of 2023, witnessed the rapid progress firsthand, and was largely convinced that within a few years AI would be extremely powerful.

So what would we do? The first natural question to ask was: what part of mathematics would AI be good at first? Our guess was that it would be good at coding before theorem proving, and that formally verifying research-level mathematics in Lean might one day be possible. The issue was that neither of us knew any Lean. However, Jaume, being Jaume, quickly responded with “No problem, I’ll just teach a course on it”.

I attended Jaume’s Lean course in Fall 2025. We began by playing the Natural Number Game, then learned some of the theory behind formal verification, and finally proceeded to read and write Lean proofs. The class was extremely fun; I see why people often compare writing proofs in Lean to playing an addictive strategy game. That said, it is also important to mention that I was likely the worst student in the class. Indeed, my programming experience is limited, I had to miss several lectures due to travel, and I may have “forgotten” to return some of my homework. I mention this to put the time commitment in perspective. Roughly speaking, 10 hours of class time was sufficient for me to later confidently check (once LLMs became good at coding) that my research papers were formalized correctly.

In February 2026 I received a message from Jaume, now at NYU Data Science, enthusiastically suggesting that formalizing papers in Lean with LLMs should be possible. He was right, and within one month we had two of our joint papers in Lean. This was a shocking experience for me, and my first reaction was to tell as many people as I could. Although convincing people in March that the AI revolution had already begun was not so easy, I am happy to say that more than a dozen members of our community have now verified their papers in Lean!

There are two other major contributors to our Lean effort who are worth mentioning explicitly: David Muñoz-Lahoz and Lukas Liehr. David is the creator and maintainer of our community Lean library in Banach lattice theory. His journey to Lean also began in 2025, when, for fun, he verified Kakutani’s C(K)C(K)-representation theorem, arguably the most fundamental result in Banach lattice theory. When I told him that Lean code could now be written with AI, he immediately began working on creating a high-quality reusable library for our field. Within two months, he had already put the core theory of Banach lattices in the library, and then began teaching others how to contribute. Lukas, on the other hand, had no experience with Lean before March 2026. However, he became completely fluent in just a few weeks, and has now produced several million lines of Lean code. The workflows and advice for formalizing papers and libraries that I present here have been largely influenced by their feedback. I also benefited from discussions with many other researchers, including Susanna Bertolini, Cynthia Bortolotto, Henry Cohn, Enric Florit-Simon, Bogdan Georgiev, Javier Gómez-Serrano, Josef Greilhuber, Liudmyla Kryvonos, Pedro Tradacete, and Peiyang Yu.

2. How Lean can be used

In February, autoformalizing a paper in Lean was far from trivial, and the code was extremely poor quality. However, over the last nine months the barrier to entry has dropped significantly (assuming you have access to a frontier LLM) and the code quality has improved dramatically. Here, I will give some examples demonstrating why formal verification is important and why one should learn it now.

2.1. Some ways that I use Lean

I will focus mainly on applications of “autoformalization”, where an LLM writes the Lean code with little human input, and “semi-autoformalization”, where a human guides the definitions and statements. However, before proceeding, it is important to remark on the numerous benefits of human-led formal verification. Indeed, Mathlib-level formalization yields perhaps the deepest understanding of a given theorem, as it forces one to consider the most effective way to state it, the most efficient way to execute its proof, the best use of tactics, and the potential reusability of the code. In contrast, I tend to use semi-autoformalization to explore the large-scale geometry of a proof or a research field, and autoformalization to quickly check that a theorem is correct.

  1. Checkpoints and generalizations. One way we use formal verification is to establish “checkpoints” which allow us to take bigger risks and be more creative. For example, a typical 100+ page PDE paper naturally divides into 5 or 6 sub-objectives (linear theory, difference estimates, energy estimates, etc.) which are essentially decoupled. One of the stressful parts of writing such a paper is that all of these pieces must come together at the end, and a mistake in one can make progress in the others less interesting. Nowadays, however, once we have an informal proof of one of the sub-objectives, we can quickly verify it in Lean. This then gives confidence that the sub-objective is complete and additional motivation for closing the other objectives.

    We have similarly used Lean to generalize proofs. For example, in our paper on L2L^2-stability of STFT phase retrieval, we initially proved what could be thought of as the case (n,p,d)=(0,1,1)(n,p,d)=(0,1,1) of a much more general theorem. We extended the result in several steps, verifying each partial extension in Lean and then using it to take the next step. This eventually led to an all-encompassing theorem whose proof was more than double the length of the original.
  2. Presenting math in new ways. Formal verification also offers the possibility of presenting math in new ways. For example, in the paper on STFT phase retrieval mentioned above, the core ideas were already present in the case (n,p,d)=(0,1,1)(n,p,d)=(0,1,1), and although the general case was practically useful, the proof was essentially just a technical exercise in bookkeeping. Formal verification presents an interesting opportunity: could mathematicians in the future spend most of the paper explaining the main ideas and then relegate technical details to an appendix or GitHub repository with a formal certificate that the details are correct? This may be a very natural way of presenting mathematics, as experts can focus on the main ideas and students can still have access to the details together with a guarantee that they will work out.
  3. Expediting the tedious parts of math. For me, one of the least instructive but most time-consuming stages of writing a paper happens when all of the sub-objectives are complete but have to be glued together. I have had several experiences where my collaborators and I had to finish writing a long paper before one of us was on the job market. We knew the proof would work, but getting all of the constants and design choices to globally align took hundreds of hours. This was neither fun nor instructive, and the combination of LLMs and Lean can help automate this process. Indeed, one can ask the LLM to put the pieces together and Lean verify the resulting blueprint. One can then analyze the Lean code to decide which design choices work and which cause issues, and then implement the most pleasing ones in the paper. One can also see more clearly how constants propagate through the argument, and how refinements of the method could improve the constants.
  4. Performing intractable computations. The combination of LLMs and Lean may help in connecting mathematics to the other sciences by making it possible to study models that are too complicated to analyze by hand. There are also likely many problems that were not worth spending time on (such as optimizing constants or doing a large case analysis) that can now be solved quickly by LLMs, verified in Lean, and stored as useful data. This could lead to new “experimental” ways of doing mathematics.
  5. Learning new math faster. Another use case is to learn new mathematics at an unprecedented rate while certifying that your understanding is correct. As an example, my collaborators and I were recently working on a conjecture in time-frequency analysis which we believed to be false, but disproving it would require topological facts that lie outside of our area of expertise. We therefore asked GPT-5.4 which topological obstructions might disprove the conjecture. It suggested that we use Chern classes, and after learning more about them, we realized that they were indeed the right tool. We then wrote an argument disproving the conjecture. Although we were quite confident that the argument was correct, we still felt a bit nervous, as we were using techniques that we had only recently learned. We therefore autoformalized our proof in Lean, confirming that our understanding of the subject was solid.

    More generally, LLMs can serve as a personal tutor that allows the user to explore new techniques and fields exceptionally fast. The caveat, of course, is that there is no certificate of correctness in their arguments. Five months ago, this was blatantly obvious, as the LLMs would frequently hallucinate. Now, it is less obvious, but even the most advanced models still make subtle mistakes. Since finding these mistakes is by no means fun, I personally prefer to Lean verify any major claim produced by an LLM before I commit too much of my time to understanding the argument.
  6. Organizing knowledge, building community and enhancing morale. Lean libraries serve as a way to organize knowledge. Through the process of semi-autoformalizing the Banach lattice library, the contributors obtained a remarkable understanding of the geometry of their field, leading to new mathematical discoveries and unforeseen connections. Incorporating Lean into our workflows has also united our community, as teaching Lean, building libraries, and formalizing papers all require substantial communication. These interactions have led to a noticeable boost in morale, especially among young people, who have been particularly enthusiastic about learning Lean.

    Formal verification also offers the potential for large-scale projects, as researchers from different communities can now confidently contribute to resolving an interdisciplinary problem without having to be an expert in all aspects of the problem. I suspect that this will lead to very interesting ways of doing research in the future.
  7. Refereeing and checking proofs. In the last few months, the number of papers on arXiv has more than doubled, placing a huge burden on referees. I believe that formal verification will soon become a standard component of the refereeing process, and that there will be an increasing demand for mathematicians who can check formal statements.

    Formal verification can similarly be used to catch errors in the existing literature. Although the mathematical literature is generally reliable, it is not perfect, and this can be exploited. For example, my colleagues recently told me that an LLM “solved” one of the major open problems in Banach lattice theory. Although the reasoning of the LLM was entirely correct, it relied on a reference that turned out to be wrong. A benefit of autoformalization is that it can not only check proofs and references, but also pinpoint exactly where a gap occurs.

2.2. Some uses of Lean outside of mathematics.

Formal verification is becoming increasingly important in industry. Major companies such as Amazon and Microsoft use it extensively to certify that their software does what it is intended to do. This work has recently become urgent, as AI can now find and exploit vulnerabilities in critical software. It is therefore essential both to identify existing bugs and to formally verify that critical software meets its specifications. The recent Anthropic post

https://www.anthropic.com/research/formal-verification

explains the problem well; this seems like an area where mathematicians familiar with formal verification could make a substantial contribution.

Formal verification also has the potential to impact numerous other branches of science and technology. I suspect that different areas of STEM may soon blend together, with mathematics and Lean giving a rigorous basis for discovery and verification. For example, large-scale numerics and computer-assisted proofs are now often AI-assisted. However, if AI writes the code, it becomes difficult for humans to review it all. One fix is to write additional Lean code to verify that the original AI-assisted code is correct. Although this may sound promising, it is easier said than done. Indeed, in my experience, verifying a computer-assisted proof in Lean (without using native_decide) is considerably harder than formalizing a conventional proof. This suggests that substantial effort will be needed before formal verification can be performed at a pace and cost comparable to writing the original code.

Finally, I will mention that formal verification is playing an increasingly important role in the development of AI itself. In AI safety, formal verification can, in principle, be used to ensure that AI systems satisfy certain safety properties. Formal proofs are also commonly used to train LLMs, through reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. For better or worse, proving and formally verifying theorems in Lean is also an effective way to benchmark LLMs and advertise their capabilities.

3. Verification versus understanding

In February and March, the process of autoformalization was quite illuminating. Indeed, we had one example where we could not get the LLMs to verify a (correct) proof, as it relied on too many external references and compactness arguments. We therefore had to find a new, more elementary and quantitative proof that was easier to verify in Lean. This was extremely instructive, as it helped us better understand the problem we were tackling and the limitations of our methods.

However, it is now possible to prompt an LLM for a solution to a problem and use Lean to verify that the solution is correct, all without understanding the proof. I would argue that this is a double-edged sword. In some cases, it is great to know that a result is true and that experts can, in principle, work to understand the proof. Often, though, the person who solved the problem also matters, as someone invested in the problem is naturally motivated to explore follow-up questions or find a simpler proof. In my own research, the problems that I leave open are often not the ones I want to solve most, but the ones blocking me from the questions I find even more interesting. Unfortunately, our current reward system gives greater recognition to resolving a named conjecture than to developing the theory that follows from its solution. I hope that in the future we will find new ways to encourage the development of complete theories, and have better venues to disseminate and organize them.

A related point is that Lean does not distinguish between two proofs of the same theorem; the technical term for this is proof irrelevance. Of course, this is not how mathematicians view proofs, as different proofs often give different perspectives, insights, and hints toward future results. It is therefore natural to ask how best to present multiple proofs (both formal and informal) in an organized manner, and how to reward the production of instructive proofs, even when Lean cannot tell them apart. More broadly, I find it exciting to think about creative ways in which formal artifacts can deepen our understanding of mathematics, and how to build infrastructure to better organize and communicate knowledge.

4. What does the future hold?

Although the future is unpredictable, I believe that formal verification will only become more important. The recent xenaproject post How to formalize all of mathematics discussed the possibility of formalizing all of mathematics. I have very little doubt that most, if not all, of mathematics will be formally verified in the next three years.

However, if I have learned anything over the last nine months, it is that AI is advancing far faster than humans are adapting. For the formal verification of mathematics to have a maximal positive impact, I believe that it is key for mathematicians to learn how to read and use Lean now. Our tutorial serves as a guide for beginners who want to formalize papers and subject-specific libraries. I hope that this guide will convince mathematicians that medium-scale formal verification using LLMs is no longer out of reach, and that in the coming months we will see more programs, conferences, funding, and initiatives to encourage mathematicians to get up to speed on formal verification.

item.content:encoded:
This post is an attempt to explain in simple terms how to interpret claims of the form “this theorem is correct because it was checked in Lean”. I was inspired to write it after receiving some emails from Alice Silverberg asking for more details about what claims like this actually meant, and I thank her for asking me these questions. The summary is: there is an important signal that can be extracted from Lean code, but if this code is AI-generated then you need to do some tests first. We explain the tests, and note that in many cases (such as the OpenAI theorem dump) these tests have not yet been systematically done.

Introduction

Last month’s theorem dump by OpenAI consisted of 722 mathematics papers, around 45% of which came with some Lean code. Three of the (non-Leanified) papers have since been retracted because of a sign error. Some people might say “well, the papers that come with Lean code are definitely correct because that’s how Lean works”. Others might say “well Lean had a soundness bug and could well have more, and AIs will reward hack, so Lean verification doesn’t tell us much at all”. The truth, unsurprisingly, is more subtle, and this post is an attempt to explain it.

This post is structured as a sequence of four questions that one needs to ask about a Lean repository, particularly if it is AI-generated, before one can start to make correctness claims of this form. And before I start, let me stress that for many of the papers in the OpenAI theorem dump, these questions have not yet all been answered affirmatively (but there is nothing stopping people from answering these questions, and I have no reason to believe that any of the tests below will fail, it’s just that people didn’t do them yet).

Question 1. Does the Lean statement match the informal statement?

A Lean repository will typically have a “headline theorem statement”. This will be some computer code which defines the statement (not the proof!) of a theorem. Note the huge difference here between the statement, and the proof. For example here is some fully-compiling Lean code which defines a mathematical statement.

import Mathlib
def FermatsLastTheorem : Prop := 
  ∀ a b c n : ℕ, n ≥ 3 → a^n + b^n ≠ c^n

This code imports Lean’s mathematics library Mathlib and then defines a mathematical statement which looks at first glance like it might be Fermat’s Last Theorem, but which actually is a trivially false statement because in Lean ℕ contains 0, so a = b = c = 0 and n = 3 gives a counterexample. This does not stop the statement from compiling! It will however stop any proof of this statement from compiling. Lean carefully distinguishes between the statement of a theorem and the proof of a theorem; humans are very good at referring to both ideas as “a theorem”.

The first question which one has to ask when judging a pdf which comes with some Lean code is: “what is the statement of the theorem in the Lean code, and does this correspond to the actual theorem statement in the pdf?” For a human Lean expert, this is typically (but not always) an easy question to answer. For example any Lean-competent human mathematician would be able to read the two lines of code above and observe that this was a mis-statement of Fermat’s Last Theorem.

Things are, however, not always as easy as this. Currently, because of deficiencies in available libraries, one may have to read many thousands of lines of code just to understand the statement of a formalised theorem. An example of this right now is a PR to DeepMind’s Formal Conjectures repository containing a Lean formalisation of the statement of the Hodge conjecture. At the time of writing, the statement relies on over 10,000 lines of code sitting on top of Mathlib, because Mathlib (which is carefully human-expert-checked and which can be trusted) does not yet have the definitions of things like the cycle class map needed to make the statement. Another example is Axiom’s recent announcement of a formally-verified proof of the classification of finite simple groups. The statement which Axiom’s system proved is here in Tau Ceti, an AI-generated library of Lean code. The file containing the statement imports over 250K lines of Lean code in Tau Ceti (over 900 files). Of these, around 5600 lines of code are crucial because they contain all the relevant definitions (for example, all the definitions of the sporadic simple groups, most of which are still not in Mathlib). Without human checking, one does not really know for sure that this is definitely the correct statement of the classification (and note that I have not yet met any human who claims to have carefully checked that the definitions of the sporadic groups in Tau Ceti are correct). In fact by far the strongest evidence that we have that this statement is correctly formalized is that Axiom’s code proves it!

It is worth noting that of the 290 OpenAI theorems which come with Lean code, around 38 of them have the property that the Lean code does not even state, let alone prove, the main theorem of the paper. And OpenAI never claimed that it did! They just said “here is some Lean code which goes with this paper”. Sometimes the code just states and proves some intermediate results — my impression is that OpenAI decided to go live when some of the formalizations were incomplete, so just dumped what they had. To give a concrete example: paper 194 claims to prove Lech’s multiplicity conjecture in commutative algebra, with no restriction on dimension, residue field or characteristic; this question has been open since 1960. The headline theorem in the corresponding Lean code can be checked to be Corollary 5.4 of the paper — already an impressive achievement, but not the headline result.

Question 2: does the code compile?

Once you’re convinced that you understand the statement of the theorem which the Lean code purports to prove, you (or perhaps one of your friends who has access to a beefy machine, if the code base is huge) has to actually compile the code.

When Anthropic formalized a proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in Lean, they asked me to take a look at the 13 million lines of code which they had generated. I downloaded it onto my machine, dumped it into a sandbox (because who knows what AI-generated code will do, it can in theory delete all your files) and attempted to compile it; I very quickly ran out of memory. I told Anthropic that I was unable to make any claims about what they had done until I could see the code base compiling, and they gave me temporary access to a machine with 96 cores and 500 gigs of ram. I could then compile the code.

Of course, with a more reasonably-sized codebase it is possible to compile the code on a reasonably-sized machine. For example OpenAI’s resolution of the Navier-Stokes problem is 640K lines of code and compiles fine on my laptop.

It is probably worth stressing again: do not run random Lean code on your local machine unless you sandbox it first. Lean’s mathematics library is safe to run and build upon because this is human-curated and checked by human experts. AI-generated code is not.

Question 3: does the code prove the theorem as stated?

I already talked in Question 1 about the importance of checking the statement of a theorem, so we can be sure that the code is proving the right thing. However, there is an added complication here. Ideally the statement of a theorem will be contained in a file which has very few imports beyond Mathlib, so we know we can trust it. But the proof of the theorem will necessarily import thousands and possibly millions of lines of code which nobody wants to read. How do we know for sure that there is no trick hidden in the millions of lines of proof files which redefines x^n to mean 37, and then proves that a^n + b^n ≠ c^n because the left hand side is 37+37=74 and the right hand side is 37? Or which adds a new axiom to mathematics saying that the theorem is true? Put another way — given a Challenge.lean file with only trusted code imported and the statement of a theorem, and a Solution.lean file with millions of lines of untrusted code imported and the proof of a theorem which looks identical, how do we know for sure that somewhere in the millions of lines of code there is no hack which changes the meaning of the statement, changes the rules from just the axioms of mathematics,

The one-line answer: lake comparator. You can read more about this answer here. But in short, this tool checks that the theorem stated in a trusted file and the theorem proved via untrusted imports are identical, and that only the axioms of mathematics are used in the proof.

Question 4: does the code exploit a bug in Lean’s official kernel?

This can happen. There was a soundness bug in Lean’s kernel which was fixed four hours after it was discovered, and a subsequent review of Lean’s code base by OpenAI found several more, all of which were fixed before they were announced publicly. There may in theory be more soundness bugs in Lean’s kernel. However, this does not matter.

Why not? Because Lean now has many kernels, created by users, written in many different languages, and at least one of which is formally verified to have no bugs, right down to the assembly level. If you want to make absolutely sure that there is no reward-hacking then again there is a one-line answer: lake comparator --paranoid. A malicious piece of code exploiting an as-yet-undiscovered bug in Lean’s official kernel will not pass this test unless it exploits as-yet-undiscovered bugs in many independent systems all at once. For example this webpage from the Lean kernel arena demonstrates that OpenAI’s resolution of the Navier–Stokes problem is accepted by multiple kernels as well as Lean’s official kernel.

One final remark

Even if the Lean code compiles and passes all these tests, and is thus overwhelmingly likely to be a correct proof of a theorem, this does not mean that any corresponding pdf also contains a correct proof! The Navier–Stokes lost in translation paper demonstrates the opposite in fact, for the Navier-Stokes write-up; whilst all the tests above have been run for the Navier–Stokes work, there are instances where the pdf proof and the Lean proof diverge. In these cases, who knows if the pdf proof is OK! My understanding is that some experts have been using AI to informalise the Lean proof back into English in order to read the argument, rather than ploughing through the slop in the pdf.

Summary/conclusions

“It’s true because it’s checked in Lean” can be made to make sense. But one has to do some work beyond “the Lean code compiles”. Your frontier AI model can do all of this work. But it needs to be done, and (depending on the amount of Lean code in the proof) it may be computationally costly.

item.content:encoded:
[Everyone is doing guest posts these days, so here’s one about the Weil conjectures from (in alphabetical order) Bin Dong, Nailin Guan, Jiedong Jiang, Ruochuan Liu, Christian Merten, Xiangyu Pan, Tingxiao Shi, Bin Wu, Edison Xie and Wei Yang]

We mathematicians need to put far greater effort into communicating mathematical ideas. To accomplish this, we need to pay much more attention to communicating not just our definitions, theorems, and proofs, but also our ways of thinking.

William P. Thurston, On Proof and Progress in Mathematics (1994)

Since the beginning of mathematical study, people have been trying to present mathematics and to communicate mathematical ideas. Mathematicians carefully choose names and symbols that match their intuitions in order to improve understanding. For most of this history, the medium for writing down a piece of mathematics has been linear text: a paper consisting of definitions, theorems, and proofs. In modern mathematics, however, the size and complexity of proofs and of the ideas behind them have grown rapidly. These now demand more and more effort both to write and to read.

Various efforts have been made to reorganize and represent mathematics to enhance our understanding. The Bourbaki [1] group maintains a series of textbooks developing mathematics in a coherent way. The Stacks Project [7] is an online textbook in algebraic geometry, in which theorems and definitions are tagged, linked and organized hierarchically by topic. Kerodon [3] is a similar website for higher category theory. Kedlaya’s web-based notes [2] offer another example in p-adic cohomology.

Two further examples are worth noting. The nLab [6] is a collaborative wiki with an emphasis on ideas and abstract viewpoints. It is not organized hierarchically following the logical structure of proofs, but around concepts and their relations. Mathlib [5] on the other hand is a uniform formal library organized by mathematical field and containing every detail of proofs.

Two Layers of Mathematics

The last two expositions mentioned above represent two equally indispensable components of mathematics. On one side are the analogies, the slogans, the examples and even the hand-waving arguments that carry mathematical understanding. On the other side are the rigorous, detailed proofs that refine and realize vague ideas into sound arguments. We often think in the first style and write in the second. Consider an example from probability theory. If X and Y are independent random variables, then

Var⁡(X+Y)=Var⁡(X)+Var⁡(Y).\operatorname{Var}(X+Y)=\operatorname{Var}(X)+\operatorname{Var}(Y).

A completely rigorous proof is easy to write down. Yet what guides us in proving and using this lemma is the picture of Pythagoras’ theorem.

We argue that mathematical understanding needs both: High-level ideas and rigorous proofs. Slogans and analogies can convey why a proof strategy may work, but a strategy remains a strategy as long it has not been executed as a complete proof. A text consisting only of slogans walks on clouds. It may hold one up for a step or two, and then one falls. Conversely, a perfectly detailed proof alone does not provide a picture of the whole. This is precisely why reading a proof generated by AI can be so painful. Every step is correct, yet one has no sense of the underlying motivation.

Explaining the high-level picture is similar to telling a story. However, adding storytelling into professional mathematical texts has been hard for several reasons. Choosing and computing a representative example takes effort. Worse, slogans and analogies are very easy to get wrong, and most people would rather not write at all if what they write is potentially wrong. And many proofs are conceptually clear, with the difficulty entirely technical. If one pushes through those technical difficulties to obtain a rigorous proof, that is what gets published. But nobody publishes the other text, saying “here is the argument I first had in mind, here is where it fails, and here is the repair.” This is also why people benefit much more from talking to mathematicians than from reading papers.

The situation has improved recently. Large language models (LLMs) and agents are now extremely good at figuring out proofs and filling in tedious details. The technology of formalization guarantees the correctness of every detail by having a proof assistant check each step. LLMs are also improving rapidly at auto-formalization, to reduce manual formalization work. We are in a position to see AI reduce, rather than increase as at present, the burden of presenting mathematics, so that the two layers of mathematics can be brought together in one place, connected to each other.

A Prototype

For a large proof such as the Weil conjectures, one starts from a top-level picture consisting of the analogies, dictionaries, and strategies described above. A central idea is to construct a suitable cohomology theory, and ℓ\ell-adic cohomology provides such a theory, yielding the rationality and functional equation immediately. The Riemann hypothesis part would follow from a deeper ingredient, namely the theory of weights.

One then elaborates the argument, working out what is needed at each step and how it is actually established. On the cohomological side, properties such as duality and trace formulas are developed using the six-functor formalism on the (pro-)étale site, together with calculations involving f!f^!. On the arithmetic side, Deligne’s arguments provide the weight estimates that cannot be obtained from the formalism alone.

Step by step, the slogan-level argument is refined into something checkable down to the last detail. Through this process, the vague story becomes a completely rigorous proof, and along the way one meets and resolves technical obstructions.

As a concrete proposal, we have built a prototype that attempts to organize and present a complete proof of the Weil conjectures in this way. It produces an artifact with two halves. The first is a multi-layered text presented as a website, a proof written at several levels of granularity and obtained by refining the top-level argument downwards, so that a reader can enter at whatever level of detail they want. The second is a formal artifact associated with the text, in which every step at the finest level is checked by a proof assistant, so that the whole proof is machine-verified.

This layered structure also determines the division of labour between humans and AI. Humans discuss and decide the overall proof route (see this detailed discussion), as well as the underlying key definitions and mathematical frameworks. As the argument is refined, LLMs begin to fill in the details of key theorems fixed by hand, while humans review and adjust. At the bottom, AI takes the human-readable but not yet fully rigorous text and expands every last detail on its own, then checks the result by formalization. Mathematical judgement thus sets the route, and AI makes it practical to carry the details all the way down to a machine-checked proof.

We also invested human effort in formalizing the main framework of derived categories and the six operations on the (pro-)étale site, providing an early application in Riou’s work [4] on the formalization of derived categories and derived functors, and sharing human experience dealing with potential kernel performance issues (see this detailed discussion). The formalization of detailed proofs is left entirely to auto-formalization. The bottom layer is one that a human could, but never has to, look at. People read the layer suited to them, which is compressed, comprehensible, and already detailed enough to show how the strategy actually works, knowing that the layer beneath it has been checked, so the proof is sound.

We use a website to present the notes and the formalization together. It has a graph that displays both refinement relations and proof dependencies. A high-level node can be expanded into a box containing its refining nodes, and proof dependencies are drawn as arrows. Each node corresponds to a page, with high-level nodes carrying the story and low-level nodes carrying precise proofs linked to their formal counterparts. The website thus allows readers to enter at their desired level of detail and move between exposition and machine-checked proof. The webpages can also be reconstructed into conventional linear notes.

All of this has become practical only through recent advances in LLMs and agents. Their mathematical proving ability helps elaborate the layered notes, auto-formalization capability helps complete the formal verification, and coding ability helps build the website presentation. In all three parts, humans only determine the high-level strategy and goals, while AI implements the details. This collaboration allows us to realize a modern reorganization of mathematics.

An Entangled Web of Mathematics

This is an early attempt to create a library combining both natural and formal language. Although the current prototype is built around a single huge proof of the Weil conjectures, we see it as extensible in the manner of the Stacks Project. Developing a new related body of theory, such as perverse sheaves or nearby and vanishing cycles, means that by the same process of refinement, the new proof decomposes into new parts and reusable parts already in the library. The same low-level details are organized into new high-level stories. In the dependency graph, this corresponds to adding or deleting some blocks while existing low-level blocks move around and regroup into new high-level blocks. Numerous mathematical ideas can be intertwined and linked with the shared details that support them. In this way, we weave an entangled web of mathematics.

We hope that more, and in time perhaps most, of mathematics can be reorganized in a multi-layered way. To make this practical, we need to summarize and share transferable experiences from such projects, so that human effort becomes more efficient and can be concentrated on the highest-level mathematical decisions. Imagine a comprehensive library of natural-language mathematics in which countless top-level core ideas are written down, displayed, expanded, and grounded in detail, and in which the bottom is guaranteed correct by formalization. If we could work on mathematics in this way, thinking and writing at the top level, collaborating with AI to fill in the middle, and letting AI handle the bottom entirely automatically, it might be a fascinating new way to study and understand or even extend the entangled web of mathematics.

  2. Kiran S. Kedlaya. Notes on Prismatic Cohomology (visited 5 November 2026).
  3. Jacob Lurie. Kerodon (visited 5 November 2026).

item.content:encoded:
(This is a guest post, written by Jeremy Avigad, Kevin Buzzard, Johan Commelin, Rémy Degenne, Kim Morrison, Oliver Nash and Adam Topaz.)

Mathematicians’ reactions to last week’s big OpenAI release range from excitement to frustration, but one thing is clear: AI has become remarkably good at proving theorems, both formally and informally. The successes in the formal realm have led AI enthusiasts to declare that now is the time to formalize all of mathematics as a legacy for future generations.

We are sympathetic to this proposal. We recognize the power of new technologies for mathematical reasoning and appreciate what they can contribute to the subject we know and love. We are generally optimistic about the role AI can play, but we are deeply concerned by some recent calls to formalize everything as quickly as possible. If done well, a large-scale, coordinated formalization effort could enormously expand mathematical exploration and discovery. Done poorly, it will be, at best, a waste of resources; more likely, it will do lasting damage.

We prefer to see formalization done well. This post therefore clarifies our concerns, describes some of our experiences with AI and formalization, and offers a positive vision of how we can all work toward a world in which all, or almost all, mathematical definitions, theorems, and proofs are equipped with a formal representation, and in which these artifacts help mathematics flourish.

Just as the role of AI in mathematics is a fraught subject these days, so too is its role in formalization. The range of attitudes among expert formalizers toward AI is as wide as the range of attitudes among mathematicians more broadly. We are aware that some of our closest friends and colleagues, whose opinions we value and respect highly, stand strongly opposed to large-scale formalization using AI. Nothing we say here should be taken as representative of the views of any of the organizations or communities with which we are associated.

The concerns

Let’s start with the observation that a formal artifact is not worth much if nobody uses it. When Math, Inc. tried to hijack a project to formalize Maryna Viazovska’s higher-dimensional sphere-packing results last February, it impressively demonstrated what the technology could do, but beyond that, it contributed nothing to mathematics. The original project team kept preparing a quality formalization of the 8-dimensional result and soon discovered that cleaning up the AI-generated code was more trouble than it was worth; it turned out it was better to throw the code away and do it right, still with ample help from AI.

When Anthropic announced that Claude had formally verified Fermat’s Last Theorem with 13 million lines of code written over 11 days, Kevin Buzzard cheerfully lauded the result while also declaring he had no intention of ending his ongoing formalization of a more modern proof. Once again, although the accomplishment is impressive, this piece of AI-generated code probably has little ongoing value.

What is going on here? The theorems were not seriously in doubt, so the value of the formal artifacts lies solely in what we get beyond mere correctness. We want to formalize everything because we want to use the formalizations to do more mathematics, and to do it better than we could have done without them. We want to think about possible generalizations, explore connections between different branches of mathematics, and consider unexpected applications. We want to refactor and improve our knowledge: part of the joy of manual formalization comes from realizing that we can adjust our concepts to make them more elegant, more efficient, and better suited to our purposes. Knowledge isn’t worth having until it contributes to our understanding; the value of a formalization comes from our ability to use and interact with the data.

When OpenAI announced solutions to the Navier–Stokes equations that blow up in finite time, the natural-language proof was accompanied by a Lean formalization. In contrast to the previous examples, the correctness signal played a key role here: there seems to be little doubt now that the solution is correct, even though the natural-language proof is mostly incomprehensible. OpenAI nonetheless drew the mathematics community’s anger over concerns about how it obtained the result, provenance and credit for ideas, and worries that focusing on correctness alone discouraged the exploration and understanding the Millenium prize was meant to foster. So, even here, the unadorned formal artifact is a mixed blessing. OpenAI’s later dump contains astonishing and important mathematics, and at the same time shows a remarkable disregard for readers and for building understanding (some results have been retracted, many of the informal/formal pairs diverge in subtle or significant ways, and most of the informal writeups are impenetrable).

This explains our concern. If spending millions of dollars to formalize mathematics results in libraries nobody uses, it will be a terrible waste of resources. Worse, the project could disincentivize good research and productive use of AI, disrupt the social norms and practices research depends on, and set the field back decades. A grand failure will make it hard, or even impossible, to recover later. A lousy formalization of existing results is worse than no formalization at all.

The positives

Some of the results from the big labs have been done well: OpenAI’s unit distance conjecture work, and Anthropic’s work on the density of Riemann zeta zeroes stand out. They demonstrated impressive new capabilities, contributed to understanding, and the community subsequently built on their work. These are examples of how the labs can contribute positively and we invite further constructive partnerships between the research community and the labs.

Good formal libraries will enable the positive vision we have for the future of mathematical research. Humans, AIs, and the Lean language work in concert. Today, AIs are extremely capable in many aspects of mathematical research. Researchers using interactive theorem provers already understand and appreciate the power of having a compiler that can check1 the validity of a proof. Together, these tools are incredibly effective. The AIs will generate formal proofs as they work, constantly checking these against the Lean compiler, and automatically pruning incorrect reasoning. To realize this vision, we will need a high-quality, comprehensive library of formalized mathematics at an unprecedented scale, so mathematicians can work effectively at the frontiers of research. While we are writing as research mathematicians, we must keep in mind that this vision extends beyond mathematics, potentially accelerating research in engineering and science. If and only if we do it right, that payoff would justify a very large investment of resources.

Lessons so far

We have argued that if we want to use AI to help with formalization, we need to solve a special case of the alignment problem, namely, ensuring that formal libraries fulfill the community’s mathematical goals. We believe that solving this case will provide powerful lessons about how we can more generally use AI in ways that are safe, reliable, and support our values.

How can we do that? None of us know with certainty: that is part of what makes life on the frontier both exciting and unnerving. But collectively we have experience using AI for formalization, and we should expect any serious effort to pay attention to what we have learned so far. In particular, we want to call attention to the following projects.

Mathlib is an open-source community-driven library that supports the formal mathematical ecosystem and was awarded the 2026 Jean-Pierre Demailly Prize for Open Science in Mathematics. It is curated by a team of 65 reviewers and 950 contributors to date. Because it emphasizes high-quality, trustworthy code and human curation, Mathlib grows steadily, but more slowly than AI-generated libraries. For the same reasons, it has been the primary place where we learn how to formalize better.

Formal Conjectures is a collaborative effort to collect the formal statements of open problems. This is a social enterprise that requires discussion, review, and auditing. AIs can be useful adjuncts, but the goal is to obtain trustworthy statements of the important open questions in various disciplines. We should encourage projects announcing formalizations to use the existing vetted statements of problems wherever possible.

The Annals Challenge. Kevin Buzzard is leading a project to state (but not prove) all the theorems from recent issues of Annals of Mathematics (and later other top journals). The blocker here is missing definitions, and one of the points of the project is that it incentivises good formalizations of definitions which are being used in practice by leaders of the field. Projects like this help us focus effort where it has the highest payoffs.

Tau Ceti is building a large coherent library of formal mathematics, incubated by the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative. While structurally similar to Mathlib, all contributions are written by AIs, and then adversarially reviewed by other AIs using standard rubrics. These contributions follow roadmaps curated by mathematicians and formalization experts. The review criteria include appropriate generality, avoiding duplication by reusing existing material, documentation, and naming conventions. Tau Ceti extends Mathlib without any duplication, and defers to all design decisions made there. It is possible to contribute to Tau Ceti either by writing roadmaps or by supplying inference2. Tau Ceti is now slightly larger than Mathlib (3 million lines of code), and growing rapidly. Recent results include Riemann-Roch, Schur-Weyl duality, Jordan-Brouwer separation, Rellich-Kondrakov compactness, and Chebotarev density.

Formal Frontier is a Mathlib Initiative project building a pipeline converting source texts into interlinked formal libraries. It uses an interacting community of AI agents that can be instructed to formalize specific texts. This system is designed with scalability in mind, so it can ingest thousands of textbooks. There are now 41 released libraries (e.g. on profinite groups, toric ideals, and homological algebra) comprising approximately 200k lines of code. In addition to providing infrastructure to manage the agent swarm, the Formal Frontier project has written a build server for large Lean projects. Recent highlights from Formal Frontier include formalizations of the hairy ball theorem, Kaplansky’s theorem on projective modules, Bass’s stable range theorem, Tate periodicity, and Stone duality for spectral spaces.

Formal Frontier and Tau Ceti both use agents and adversarial review, but they differ in their drivers and output structure. Tau Ceti uses roadmaps curated by experts and builds a single coherent library. Formal Frontier is primarily a source-to-library pipeline. Both insist that a formalization is only valuable if others can build on top of it. We anticipate that future autoformalization projects will build upon both approaches.

Palomar is an online registry of formal mathematics projects. The goal of Palomar is to index formalization projects aimed at particular results, but not necessarily aspiring to be part of a general library. Many such results have recently been “dumped” on GitHub, and it can be very difficult to interpret or trust them. Palomar addresses this problem by requiring two features in every project it indexes. First, the project must contain a formalization.yaml file, a metadata file containing a self-assessed description of what was formalized, how it was formalized (e.g. solely by humans, in conjunction with AIs, or autonomously by AIs), and also relationships to other work, and how the authors of the underlying informal research were involved in the project. Second, the project must include a Comparator setup, which makes it easier to audit exactly what the statement proves.

Mathlib, Tau Ceti, and Formal Frontier aspire to common values. These are not specific to autoformalization, but rather principles that apply to all formal libraries. The Mathlib community has recently published a document on values, and this is the starting point for our own list.

  1. Defer to human-curated libraries, particularly Mathlib; follow their design principles and code rules, and continuously refactor to adopt their decisions.
  2. Prefer thoroughness and breadth. These must come before depth, but ultimately enable it.
  3. Avoid duplication. Generalize theorems for maximal reuse.
  4. Review additions publicly, according to agreed standards.
  5. Publish freely. Libraries should be open source, interoperable, and explorable.
  6. Stay up to date. Ensure continuous compatibility with every release of Lean and Mathlib.
  7. Stay open-minded about changes. If a better approach is discovered, it’s never too late.
  8. Document and organize. Files should be coherent, systematically organized, and their contents must be documented.
  9. Link to the existing literature. A mathematician should be able to trust and verify that the concepts described in the library have the expected meaning.
  10. Set standards, and meet them. Producing low-quality or unaudited code and claiming or hoping to “clean it up later” is counterproductive.

Mathlib implements these values through its review process and community discussions. Tau Ceti and Formal Frontier instantiate these values in the code and prompts that drive them, as well as in community-written planning documents.

The way forward

Within three years, and possibly much sooner, most of mathematics can be formalized in such a way that mathematicians can explore, build on, and make use of formal libraries. This would significantly extend our ability to develop and discover new mathematics. The Lean FRO is committed to ensuring that Lean is able to support projects at this scale. Achieving this ambitious project will require several types of additional support and community participation:

  • Curate and contribute to Mathlib, the foundation of the formal mathematics ecosystem, where we discover best practices in formalization.
  • Provide the resources needed for the shovel-ready projects, Tau Ceti and Formal Frontier, to grow by an order of magnitude in a matter of months.
  • Write the expert roadmaps and blueprints that guide the implementation of large formal libraries. Propose and support workshops to design and improve subject-specific libraries.3
  • Develop credible modeling of the financial, engineering, and technical requirements for scaling.4
  • Advocate for control by mathematicians of the tools and resources required for autoformalization.
  • Launch non-profit or academic hosting for the mathematicians, engineers, and inference required for implementation of large-scale formalization, with the necessary governance and advisory bodies.
  1. ︎
  2. Anyone can help build Tau Ceti by running
    uv tool install git+https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiWorker followed by
    tauceti work --loop (You need `claude` or `codex`, and the `gh` GitHub command line tool authenticated.)
    ︎
  3. This is already happening, e.g. meetings on statistics and physics at ICARM, analysis at ICERM, and PDEs at SLMath. ︎
  4. We’re planning on delivering models based on Tau Ceti and Formal Frontier as soon as possible, but this is out of scope for a blog post. ︎

item.content:encoded:
Recent events in the field of AI for mathematics have shown us beyond all reasonable doubt that the field is currently undergoing a rapid transformation, unlike anything that we have ever seen before. Language models are solving hard problems which humans could not, and mathematicians are reacting very differently to this news. I personally am extremely excited about the future of our field. However it is becoming clear to me that my views are not shared by everyone in the community: indeed, many of my colleagues seem to be upset. So let me start by outlining my understanding of their positions.

The AI pessimists.

Elisabeth Kübler-Ross’ model of the process of grief is now well-known: the five stages are denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance. The first four of these are currently very well-represented within the mathematical community, and perhaps give some weight to the claim that many mathematicians are currently grieving what they perceive as a loss of something much beloved to them. However there will also be some mathematicians whose viewpoints will fall into the following categories and who will probably strongly argue that what they are feeling is not grief at all. We are not all grieving. But many of us are in one of the stages of grief.

Denial

The Association for Human Mathematics prominently states that its goal is to protect mathematics as a human endeavor against what it calls the “threat of artificial intelligence”. Members commit to not publishing AI-generated outputs, and there is an “AI-free” option to completely renounce the use of AI in a research capacity and commit to finding proofs and exploring examples without using these tools at all. From talking to its members, my understanding is that there are multiple motivations for joining this association, ranging from serious concerns about what AI is doing to mathematics, to serious concerns about what AI is doing to the planet or what it might do to humanity. A prominent member of the association is Fields Medallist Peter Scholze, who in the recent Heidelberg Laureate Forum panel on AI and mathematics said that he will not use AI and furthermore he will “die on that hill, and be some public figure that dies on that hill”. You can listen to his reasons here.

Anger

The proofs and prompts website contains posts which represent a wide variety of opinions, and it is not difficult to find posts by people who are angry. One prominent example is Vlad Lazic’s post here. Lazic has outlined his views in more detail here and that site contains several links to pieces written by other mathematicians who have similar feelings.

Bargaining

The Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence are an independent committee of senior mathematicians (including three Fields Medallists) who on Tuesday released recommendations in response to the news that OpenAI is sitting on “a large number of significant results in mathematics that they report have been produced by their internal model”. One quote from the first paragraph of the recommendation is that the group “do not endorse this practice, and we ask [the frontier AI labs] to stop testing advanced mathematical problems on proprietary models.” They go on to ask the labs to release results “responsibly” and suggest various courses of actions that the labs could consider going forwards, such as “to provide support, including funding, for the development of human understanding of the AI mathematical output that they release.” I’ll come back to these “significant results”, and also the phrase “human understanding”, later.

Depression

If you are a mathematician then you almost certainly already know at least one person who feels like this. A faculty member I know who works in fluids told me that the Navier–Stokes news was “extremely depressing”. A post-doc I know told me that they were considering leaving mathematical research because of what it was about to become. A PhD student I know told me that they were stuck on a lemma in their research and ChatGPT one-shotted it and it made them wonder what the point of it all was.

Interlude: why humans do mathematics.

I should first make it clear that the above list is certainly not intended to be a criticism of any of these positions; I hope I have given each one a fair treatment. Several people whose opinions I value highly are represented in the above list, and recently I have been trying to listen hard to what my possibly-grieving friends and colleagues are concerned about. But it is still the case that I wake up every morning feeling excited about the future of my field. Before I explain why, let me discuss the contentious question of why we do mathematics.

Thurston’s view of mathematics

The fact that AI can now prove hard theorems has quickly led humans to a discussion about why humans do mathematics at all. I would imagine that a few years ago, many mathematicians would have been happy to agree that the mathematics community gives out our biggest prizes and awards to the people who prove the hardest theorems. However, now AI is proving hard theorems, we seem to be spending a lot of time explaining that in fact we are giving these awards and prizes to the people whose ideas are giving us the deepest understanding of our field. It is also worth noting that at this point in time the deepest AI-generated mathematical proofs have been typically accompanied by a poorly-written pdf or no pdf at all, and perhaps an end-to-end formalization in Lean, giving super-human confidence in the correctness of the proof but little clue as to where the ideas came from, or even where the new ideas are. Again I defer to Scholze, who here points out that the Elkies–Klagsbrun construction of a rank 29 elliptic curve over the rationals came with a geometric explanation, but the new rank 30 and rank 31 elliptic curves came with equations and nothing else. “We didn’t learn anything really”.

The oft-cited justification of the “it’s not about the theorem tally, it’s about the human understanding” framing of our field is Thurston’s 1994 essay “On proof and progress in mathematics”, and indeed Tao’s blog now carries a quote from this essay as the splash at the top. As one can imagine, this framing of the “point” of mathematics has been met with some cynicism on social media, and even claims that mathematicians are moving the goalposts in a desperate attempt to survive. However this cynicism is not really justified; experts in the field have known perfectly well for decades or more that the prize-winning results give us not only a chunky new theorem to add to the pile, but also a big dollop of new understanding to go on top. To choose an example from my own field, the Wiles–Taylor–Wiles proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem simultaneously resolved a silly little 350-year old puzzle about positive integers with no applications, and gave us genuinely profound new insights into the Langlands Program, the ramifications of which are still being felt 30 years on (see Frank Calegari’s 2022 ICM talk for plenty of evidence for this claim).

Other views of mathematics

But Thurston’s view is not the only view in town. I re-read Hardy’s “A mathematician’s apology” this week. I first attempted to read it as an undergraduate and back then it struck me as extremely pompous and sexist; I know that the world was a different place in 1940, but I did not even make it to the end before giving up. This time I got there, and my understanding of Hardy’s viewpoint is that it is completely different to Thurston’s. Hardy is doing mathematics because he views it as art (so presumably he would be angry about AI doing mathematics for the same reasons that many artists are angry about AI doing art). He is scathing about those who “explain” (take a look at the first paragraph of the book) and frank when he tells us that one of his main motivations to prove theorems is so that he is remembered after his death. This is a view very different to Thurston’s, but also very different to my own.

Let me next discuss why promoting Thurston’s view of mathematics (which is what many of us are doing right now) may ultimately backfire on our community. AI has solved a Millennium problem and this has shown us where AI is in mathematics. But I believe that many people in our community are still vastly underestimating how fast AI is moving, perhaps because they only just started paying attention to it. If we use “understanding” as a justification for the continued existence of mathematics as a subject worth studying, then where exactly do we retreat to when in 1 year’s time AI is not only proving theorems, but also doing a perfectly good job of explaining them to humans?

I remember when I first read Thurston’s essay, and how it struck me as being rather at odds with what personally motivates me to do mathematics. I have recently been diagnosed with autism (my few friends all think that this is hilarious, having known this for decades) and I wonder whether this is one of the reasons that I hold my position. Thurston’s essay was a response to an earlier paper by Jaffe and Quinn, who argue that a mathematical idea really only becomes valid or useful once it is anchored to the ground by a rigorous proof, and they criticise some authors (including Thurston) for having important insights and then not taking the time to write down full details. My own area (the Langlands philosophy) is full of arguments which seem to be “known to the experts” without a publicly-available write-up, and this situation was what caused me to become disillusioned with the field and ultimately withdraw from curiosity-driven research completely and switch to mathematical formalization. You cannot fool Lean; one learns this very early on. Lean will not accept proof by authority or proof by intimidation; it doesn’t work like that. I feel safe with Lean.

“Understanding” mathematics.

As a PhD student of Richard Taylor in the early 1990s, I quickly understood that the statement of the theorem which I would attempt to prove in my thesis relied on a construction of Deligne attaching Galois representations to modular forms. I suggested to Taylor that I first read Deligne’s proof before continuing, and he was quick to shoot down this idea, pointing out that my funding was for 3 years only and I simply did not have enough time to get on top of all of the relevant literature at this point in my career. I never did find the time to read Deligne’s construction, or the proof of the Langlands–Tunnell theorem which was crucial in Wiles’ work, or many of the other things which I needed in my thesis and subsequent work. So do I “understand” my own work? What exactly do we even mean by “human understanding of mathematics”?

I think that whilst mathematicians are now beginning to agree that mathematics is all about human understanding, I am not entirely convinced that they will agree on what it means to understand high-level mathematics. Of course we all know it means to understand undergraduate-level results; we have taught the courses and checked everything carefully. I am able to explain all of the undergraduate algebra courses which I have ever lectured, right down to the axioms of set theory and also right down to the axioms of type theory. I understand the material in a visceral way.

But do I “understand” the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem, given that earlier this year I gave 22 hours worth of lectures on the topic? I know that Langlands–Tunnell is crucial for Wiles but I know very little about the details of what goes into it. What if there had been a mistake discovered in the process of its formalization? Can one “understand” mathematics which is wrong? Mathematics which is incomplete? I personally can not, and I personally am happy to not understand some things. I’m in it for the theorem tally. In stark contrast to Thurston, I believe that understanding is a slightly nebulous concept, whereas total number of theorems correctly proved is something which we can measure. I am well aware that I seem to be in a minority here. But I wanted to share these views anyway.

I personally call for OpenAI to simply dump their collection of theorems upon the world so that we can see exactly what they claim to have done. The tidying up can come later, and it will come later (although it will certainly come sooner if it is funded by OpenAI); in every case other than Navier-Stokes we have seen humans reverse-engineering AI-generated mathematics, and both Navier-Stokes and the new currently-secret theorems in OpenAI’s possession will be no different: if humans want to understand, we will understand. Right now humans may well be spending their time trying to prove theorems which are already proved by a tech company. Where is the logic in that? These humans have a right to know what is known. I signed this open letter urging OpenAI to simply go public with their data, because I think it is the optimal approach, given the situation we find ourselves in. If you agree then please sign it too. Sure the tech companies could make our life easier. But what is happening now is akin to censorship.

An AI optimist.

Let me now explain why I am an optimist. Time will tell us how well my opinions age.

In a 2020 piece in the Notices of the AMS, I asked the following question: “If one human had an understanding of all of modern pure mathematics simultaneously, how much further would they immediately be able to see?” Six years later we are beginning to understand the answer to this question. Machines have ingested the mathematics on the internet and are able to manipulate this data in a coherent way. The Erdős unit distance disproof came about because a machine happened to be an expert both in discrete geometry and class field theory; one rarely finds humans who are simultaneously experts in both. Machines are answering questions now which one could easily believe that humans, were they to be left alone for a few more years in the right groups, could also have answered. It’s just happening a whole lot more quickly.

Above I expressed some scepticism about mathematics being all about understanding — both the sentiment itself, and the risks that one is taking by reducing mathematics to this. My personal answer to the question of what mathematics is all about is that it’s about proving theorems (problem solving), developing tools (theory building) and seeing where to go next (conjecture formulation).

Right now we have seen a lot of evidence that computers are good at problem solving, but far less evidence of their abilities at either theory building or conjecture formulation. This puts a hard limitation on how far today’s machines will go. Time will tell us how much better tomorrow’s machines will be at these skills, and there surely will be progress, but we are yet to see anything decisive. Will there be sufficient growth in these key areas before external pressures such as cost become too great for progress to be worthwhile?

To those who dismiss the observation that machines can’t do X today with the reply that “humans just don’t understand what exponential growth looks like”, I invite you to consider the following facts. Current progress is indeed exponential, and may well continue to be exponential for a while, however we cannot expect exponential progress to continue indefinitely (exactly because of what exponential growth looks like), and furthermore mathematics is infinite which beats exponential hands down; those that don’t believe this just don’t understand what infinity looks like.

I thus believe that in the future we will reach a new “natural boundary” in mathematics, beyond (and perhaps way beyond) where we are now, but where machines are going to get stuck and where it is not viable to expend any more resources to make the next big leap. I am aware that I might be wrong. I am an optimist, so I am expecting future machines to be awesome; but I simply cannot see how they can get to infinity with finite resources, so they must stop somewhere. I believe that the optimal thing to do (at least from my personal perspective) is to let the machines loose, see what happens, and then begin the journey to where they have stopped. Things are currently moving fast. They cannot move fast forever. But if we get on board now then they will take us to extraordinary new places. And after we have arrived, the new adventure will begin.

This is why I have also signed this letter. I know that some readers will find the ideas in it abhorrent. But I cannot fail to be excited by the powerful new tools which we have. Wir müssen wissen — wir werden wissen!

item.dc:creator: xenaproject

item.content:encoded:
I guess technically it was revealed to the world by a coffee shop in Islington on Insta, but an hour later it was officially announced by Anthropic: one of their internal models, using the prove2.me platform, has formalized a complete proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem (FLT) in Lean. This is the final theorem to be formalized in Freek Wiedijk’s famous list of 100 formalization challenges and thus wraps up this 20-year-old benchmark. Congratulations to Anthropic!

Mathematical details

The proof is not the modern proof which I have been formalizing myself following ideas of Khare, Taylor etc, but the Darmon–Diamond–Taylor exposition from 1995 of the Wiles–Taylor–Wiles argument, via the Langlands–Tunnell theorem and Ribet’s level-lowering theorem. Anthropic’s repository develops Fontaine theory (to study flat deformations of Galois representations) and develops enough of Mazur’s work on the Eisenstein ideal to conclude that no Frey curve can have a point of order . This means that their FLT proof only works for , however FLT was already formalized for odd regular primes by Best–Birkbeck–Brasca–Rodriguez–van-der-Velde–Yang, and the smallest irregular prime is 37, so it’s all good.

The code base

I’ve compiled the code base and run comparator on it — it checks out. It is a gigantic proof (over 13.4 million lines of code) and takes nearly 20 times as long to compile as Lean’s mathematics library (on a machine with 96 cores!). Lean can be sluggish when jumping from file to file on a repo of this size (even on a machine with 500G of ram, which Anthropic also gave me access to), but Anthropic also supplied me with some html documents which are easier in practice to explore (clone the repo and open with a web browser).

What this work is, and is not

I am currently being funded by the EPSRC to formalize a proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem, and a naive reaction to the news above is that I no longer have any work to do. This is not the case. The work certainly achieves some of the aims of the EPSRC project, and indeed it goes much further in terms of what is formalized (I only promised the EPSRC that I would reduce FLT to the 1980s; this repo proves the whole thing). But I also promised several other things to EPSRC: firstly, that I would be making pull requests to Lean’s mathematics library, adding fundamental objects from modern number theory; this is ongoing. And secondly, and perhaps most importantly, that I would be creating a dynamic document enabling humans to explore the modern proof. My guess is that it is unlikely that Anthropic are going to do this; they will feel that their job is done with the formalization (and they did not formalize the modern proof anyway).

Note that mathematically this work of anthropic tells us essentially nothing: I am on record as saying that I am 99.9% sure that the proof of FLT is OK, and most people in the number theory community are 100% sure (formalization has made me more paranoid about the mathematical literature than most). From my understanding of the argument, the formalization just faithfully follows the early literature on the proof and adds nothing.

What this work does tell us, however, is what is possible in the field of autoformalization. If thousands of pages of the literature can be formalized end-to-end by some kind of AI swarm in an 11 day period now, then in the future we will start to see formalization of modern research being done on the fly. We will also learn whether my paranoia about the current state of the Langlands program is justified, as machines check it and ruthlessly flag arguments which are incomplete. The ability to autoformalize hard material will ultimately make the review process for mathematics papers far less painful. It will also keep us honest — there are papers out there which assume results which are “known to the experts” and it will be interesting to see exactly what is being assumed in the proofs of various important results in my field. This is why I am so excited about the news!

I was given £1M to run my project over 5 years; Anthropic took only 11 days but I do wonder if they spent more money…

An anecdote

Thought it might be nice to finish with a personal anecdote. Wiles announced his proof of FLT at the Newton Institute in 1993 in a series of three lectures; I attended the first (I was a second year graduate student at the time) and I found it completely incomprehensible, so I skipped the next two lectures and went on holiday to Ireland with my new girlfriend instead; I was so in love that I totally forgot about the rumours, and it was only when I came back to Cambridge a week later that I heard the news that the theorem was proved. Something strangely similar happened here; when I got the email from Anthropic I was in Wales at the Green Man music festival with the same girlfriend, but with very poor phone reception; I did spot an email from someone I’d never heard of in a brief moment of 4G, with title “End-to-end Lean formalization of Fermat’s Last Theorem”, but wrote them off as a crank! It was only a week later when going through the nearly 1000 unread emails which had accrued whilst I was away, that I heard the news.
